# Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute {#sec-reasoning}

@sec-post-training ended with a model that had been taught to answer. This
chapter is about a different dial: not *how much you train*, but **how much the
model is allowed to compute when the question arrives** — how many tokens it
writes before answering, how many candidate answers it produces for the same
question.

These choices can change per request, and their cost is paid at inference, as
usage grows. Their effect has to be measured on accuracy, latency and cost
together; otherwise they can be set wrong in production without ever running a
training job.

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain why writing intermediate tokens gives a transformer more computation,
  and why that is a claim about *architecture* rather than about *thinking*;
- distinguish chain-of-thought as a prompting trick from chain-of-thought as a
  trained behaviour, and say what reinforcement learning changed;
- measure how a thinking budget relates to task performance, latency and cost
  per correct answer;
- compare spending the same compute on one long answer, on several samples, or
  under a verifier;
- test where reasoning may help, task by task and model by model — from a
  measurement, not a hunch;
- examine, with interventions, how far a reasoning trace explains the answer.

## Why writing more tokens buys more computation {#sec-why-tokens-compute}

Start with the mechanism, because everything else in the chapter rests on it.
Rather than saying "the model thinks out loud", look at generation itself:
producing more intermediate tokens lets the same network run again and later
steps use the representations at earlier positions.

A transformer has a fixed number of layers. @sec-transformers built one: an
embedding, $L$ identical blocks, an output head. When the model produces a
token, the computation that produced it is $L$ blocks deep, not conditional on
difficulty. **A hard question gets the same number of layers as an easy one.**

So consider a model that must answer `48 + 48/2` in a single token. Everything
— parse, divide, add — has to happen inside those $L$ blocks, in one pass. That
does not mean a model *cannot* solve in one pass a problem whose written-out
steps outnumber its layers — a layer does a lot in parallel — but generating
intermediate tokens opens an extra path of sequential computation for some
multi-step tasks.

Now let it write first. Each token it generates is appended to the context and
fed back in, so producing the *next* token is another $L$ blocks — and those
blocks can attend to the tokens just written. Two things change at once, and
only the first is usually mentioned:

1. **Serial depth.** $n$ generated tokens mean roughly $n$ sequential
   generation steps of $L$ blocks each; the total computation and the depth of
   task that can be solved are not exactly $n \times L$, though.
2. **Working memory.** What carries forward from one position to the next is
   the per-position hidden states of the tokens already written (the keys and
   values held in the KV cache), which later positions read back through
   attention. There is no separate register file and no scratchpad off to the
   side. So writing `24` down does two jobs — it fixes the value for later steps
   to read, and it buys one more position's worth of state to compute in. Hidden
   states can also carry information beyond the visible token text.[^filler]

[^filler]: Strictly, what attention reads at an earlier position is that
position's hidden state, not the characters `24`, and a hidden state can hold
more than the token spells out. @pfau2024letsthink pushes precisely on that gap:
transformers given purpose-built supervision can solve problems using **filler**
tokens — literally `...` — hitting "100% and 94% accuracy" on two synthetic
tasks they otherwise fail. Two limits keep this a footnote rather than a
correction. It does not arise from ordinary training — "standard
chain-of-thought data is insufficient for models to learn to leverage filler
tokens effectively", and commercial models "achieve the same performance with
filler tokens as they do when responding directly". And it is bounded:
"transformers remain in TC⁰ with even a polynomial number of filler tokens".
These are results for specially supervised models, on synthetic tasks and under
theoretical assumptions; do not generalise them into every model's complexity
limit or into the necessary mechanism of natural-language chain-of-thought. The
finding earns its place here for a different reason — see @sec-faithfulness —
as a demonstration that the visible intermediate text need not record all of the
computation.

Two consequences fall straight out of this picture, and both matter later.

**A trace can be wrong in its wording and still help.** If what pays is the
extra serial computation and the values written down, then prose that
misdescribes the computation can still sit alongside a correct answer. Hold on
to this; @sec-faithfulness is where it stops being a curiosity and becomes a
governance problem.

**The value of extra tokens varies by task.** Where a direct answer suffices, a
long trace can be pure cost; on some tasks it can still allow a check or a
correction. Which effect dominates is what @sec-cot-limits measures.

**What we will look at.** You have just seen the mechanism: why producing more
tokens buys more computation, which is less obvious than it sounds. Next comes
how that went from a prompt to a trained behaviour, what a thinking budget costs in
latency, and the ways of spending it other than thinking longer. Then the two
questions a practitioner actually needs answered — where reasoning earns its
tokens, and whether the trace it prints is a record of what happened.

## Chain-of-thought: prompted, then trained {#sec-cot-two-ways}

### The prompting era

In 2022 the finding was that you could get this behaviour without retraining,
from a model not specifically trained for it (choosing examples and the extra
input tokens still cost something). @wei2022chain showed that few-shot prompts
whose worked examples included the intermediate steps changed the outputs
sharply: PaLM 540B on GSM8K went from **17.9%** with standard prompting to
**56.9%** with chain-of-thought — the paper's own delta, $+39.0$ points.

::: {#gloss-chain-of-thought .column-margin .term-gloss}
**chain-of-thought** — intermediate steps a model writes before its final
answer. It can be elicited with prompt examples or encouraged by training;
whether it lives in a separate thinking block depends on the model and how it
is served.
[↩](#term-chain-of-thought){.term-back}
:::

@kojima2022zeroshot then removed even the examples. Appending
`Let's think step by step` to the question took text-davinci-002 on GSM8K from
**10.4%** to **40.7%**. That gap belongs to that model and prompt setup; do not
expect the same sentence to do the same for another model.

Two things about that era are easy to forget, and both are in @wei2022chain
explicitly.

First, it was [chain-of-thought](#gloss-chain-of-thought){#term-chain-of-thought .term-ref} as an *emergent* effect:
"chain-of-thought prompting is an emergent ability of model scale". The paper
gives two different thresholds, and they are worth keeping apart.

Gains arrive late. Prompting "does not positively impact performance for small
models, and only yields performance gains when used with models of
$\sim$100B parameters". But harm arrives much earlier — "chain of thought
actually hurts performance for most models smaller than 10B
parameters".[^wei-scale] Small models produce fluent, confident, wrong steps.

Second, it was a *prompting* result: the weights did not change; worked
examples in the context encouraged a stepwise **form** of answer. How much of
the effect came from solution text seen in pretraining (worked problems,
textbook derivations) and how much from computation the model could already
do, this comparison alone cannot say.

[^wei-scale]: The $\sim$100B figure is from their §3.2, the 10B figure from
Appendix A.1; between the two lies a band where chain-of-thought is neither
reliably helpful nor reliably harmful. Note that no model in the sweep sits at
100B — the ladder runs GPT-3 at 350M/1.3B/6.7B/175B, LaMDA at
422M/2B/8B/68B/137B and PaLM at 8B/62B/540B, so the turn is *bracketed*
(between 8B and 62B for PaLM, 68B and 137B for LaMDA) rather than located. The
threshold is task-dependent too: gains are "larger ... for more-complicated
problems", and on SingleOp, the single-step subset of MAWPS, improvements "were
either negative or very small". These thresholds belong to the model families
studied then; they do not carry over directly to today's small models trained
for reasoning, such as this chapter's Qwen3-1.7B.

This has a specific weakness. During few-shot CoT the model is not updated; it
writes the intermediate steps as part of token generation conditioned on the
examples given. Whether those steps are correct, or causally needed for the
answer, cannot be read off their form.

### What reinforcement learning changed

The 2024–2025 shift was to stop asking and start training. @sec-preference built the
machinery: sample, score, update. Replace the human preference score with an
**automatic check of the final answer** — did the program pass its tests, is
the number right — and you can run that loop at a scale no human labelling
budget reaches. The specific algorithm R1 uses for it is **GRPO**
[@shao2024deepseekmath], which @sec-preference derives: it drops the value
network and takes its baseline from the mean reward of a *group* of samples on
the same prompt. This lightens the human-labelling load, but generating,
checking and diversifying many attempts per question still costs compute, and
the method's value depends on the reward actually separating good attempts from
bad ones.

::: {#gloss-verifiable-reward .column-margin .term-gloss}
**verifiable reward** — a training signal computed by checking the answer
automatically — a predefined condition such as the result or the format —
rather than by asking a human or a learned reward model. Qualities the checker
does not cover have to be evaluated separately.
[↩](#term-verifiable-reward){.term-back}
:::

A published account worth reading is DeepSeek-R1 [@guo2025deepseekr1], because
it shows its method in detail. Their DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained by
reinforcement learning from a base model with **no supervised warm-up at all**,
on a [verifiable reward](#gloss-verifiable-reward){#term-verifiable-reward .term-ref}. Over training, its
average pass@1 on AIME 2024 rose **from 15.6% to 77.9%**; with self-consistency
decoding — a technique @sec-parallel-compute returns to — it reached
86.7%.[^r1-version] The two numbers are not at the same inference cost: the
second needs many samples per problem and a vote.

[^r1-version]: These figures are from the Nature version of the paper, which we
cite. The first arXiv version (v1) gives the same measurement as 71.0%; the
86.7% with majority voting is the same in both.
(AIME is a hard American high-school mathematics competition whose answers are
integers, so scoring is exact. *pass@1* is the share of problems solved by a
single sampled answer, here averaged over several samples per problem.)

What makes this different in kind from prompting is *where the behaviour comes
from*. Nobody demonstrated backtracking. The reward said only "the final answer
was right", and the strategies that produce right answers were discovered.
The paper reports an "aha moment" during training, and is refreshingly concrete
about what that means empirically: it is "characterized by a sudden increase in
the use of the word 'wait'". That shows training changing the output behaviour,
with more patterns that look like stopping to re-check; on its own it does not
explain how any internal checking process works.

**A second source of reasoning: distillation.** Not every reasoning model gets
the behaviour from its own reinforcement learning. The same paper released
small "R1-Distill" models, put through supervised fine-tuning on R1's traces;
@muennighoff2025s1 made do with SFT on about 1,000 examples. This chapter's
instrument, Qwen3-1.7B, also got its ability, according to its technical
report, by strong-to-weak distillation from the large Qwen3 models rather than
from its own RL [@yang2025qwen3]. The mechanism is the knowledge distillation of
@sec-distillation; the student's performance depends on which teacher outputs
were chosen, on its own capacity and on the task measured, and has no fixed
ceiling.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The honest footnote on R1-Zero.** Pure RL from a base model did not produce a
shippable assistant. The same paper reports that R1-Zero "faces challenges such
as poor readability and language mixing, occasionally combining English and
Chinese in a single CoT response", and that its rule-based RL stage was
"narrowly focused on reasoning tasks", leaving it weak at writing and
open-domain questions. The released DeepSeek-R1 adds supervised stages around
the RL to fix exactly this.

The lesson generalises past this one model: **a reward that only checks the
answer only constrains the answer.** Everything you did not measure is free to
drift — which is @sec-forgetting's point arriving from a new direction.
:::

OpenAI's o1 [@openai2024o1] had made the commercial case a few months earlier,
in September 2024, with the figure caption that named the two dials: "o1 performance smoothly improves with
both train-time and test-time compute". Be precise about what is public here,
because a lot of writing is not: the September 2024 announcement reports that
performance improves with train-time and test-time compute; its methodological
statement is that a large-scale reinforcement learning algorithm teaches the
model to use its chain of thought. It does not give enough of the training
algorithm, the data or the reward design to reproduce them. They also chose not to show raw traces to users, citing
"user experience, competitive advantage, and the option to pursue the chain of
thought monitoring" — so in that product version what a user saw was
a *summary* of the trace, not the trace. Check current API behaviour in the
relevant documentation.

Since then, some hosted models have changed the *shape of the dial*: instead of
a token count they offer an effort level, or adaptive settings where the model
decides how long to think. Whether these settings exist, whether the trace is
visible and how it is billed vary by model version; before equating this
chapter's local token cap with a provider's API setting, check that version's
documentation. Treat every version number in this chapter as an example with a
short shelf life.

measured for both.

## Thinking budgets, latency, and the shape of the cost curve {#sec-budgets}

Some reasoning models produce their thinking tokens in a structurally separate
place — a block, delimited, generated before the answer and in many products
hidden from the person who asked. This chapter's experiment is on
`Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B`, which uses a separate `<think>` block; other models may
differ in the visible block, the control parameter or how they truncate. That
structure is what makes a **budget** possible: you can cap the block without
touching the answer.

Qwen3 makes the two modes explicit enough to experiment on, which is why this
chapter uses it. Its chat template carries an `enable_thinking` flag. With it
on, the model opens a `<think>` block, reasons, closes it, and answers. With it
off, the template inserts an *empty* `<think></think>` pair, so the model skips
straight to the answer. **Same weights, two behaviours.**

When the two modes are compared, the weights stay fixed; the chat template and
the recommended sampling settings change.[^decode] Both modes were also trained
deliberately, so neither is a neutral baseline. The results below are therefore
the difference between the two modes' recommended setups — the choice a
practitioner faces. They should not be read as the causal effect of the thinking
block alone.

**A postscript.** Since we ran this, the vendor abandoned
the design our instrument depends on: from the 2507 checkpoints onward Qwen
ships *separate* Instruct and Thinking models rather than one hybrid, on the
stated grounds that training them separately gets "the best quality possible".
The 2507 refresh covered only some sizes, with no 1.7B among them. Pin
`Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B` if you want to reproduce our numbers, and check whether
`enable_thinking` is still honoured before you trust a sweep on any newer
checkpoint with a short example — a flag that is silently ignored produces a
table that looks fine. To repeat the experiment, pin the exact model revision and
chat template as well. The separate 2507 Instruct and Thinking models are not a
stand-in for this chapter's hybrid model, and the decision to ship separate
models does not by itself explain the mode difference measured here.

[^decode]: Thinking mode runs at temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.95, top-$k$ 20;
non-thinking at temperature 0.7, top-$p$ 0.8, top-$k$ 20. These are the model
card's per-mode recommendations, and **every measurement in this chapter uses
them** — the budget sweeps, the self-consistency run and the faithfulness probe
alike. Nothing here decodes greedily. The practical consequence is that the
no-thinking row of the table below is not *only* a no-thinking row — it also
samples a little hotter and truncates the tail harder, and we have not
separated those effects from the absence of the block. The choice buys realism
— each mode runs the way its authors intend — and costs comparability, which is
the opposite trade to the one a greedy sweep would make. If you rerun the lab,
decide which of the two you want *before* you start, and say which you used.

::: {#gloss-thinking-budget .column-margin .term-gloss}
**thinking budget** — a cap or target on the tokens or compute a model may spend
inside its reasoning block before answering. In this chapter's local experiment
the cap is hard: the trace is cut, the closing tag is added and the answer is
generated in a separate phase. How hosted systems implement budgets and caps
has to be read from their own documentation.
[↩](#term-thinking-budget){.term-back}
:::

Panel B shows the *hard* cut this chapter uses: the trace is stopped, the closing
tag is added and answer generation starts. It does not represent every
provider's budget implementation. The request is not cancelled and no error is
raised; an answer comes back, on time, from an unfinished derivation. To see the
quality loss, track the truncation rate and the task result separately; latency
and error rate alone will not show it.

::::

### What you are actually paying for

Three separate costs move together when the block gets longer, and they are
charged to three different people.

**Tokens.** The tokens inside the block are generated like any others and need
computation. On a hosted service, check that model's pricing documentation for
how they enter the usage counter and the bill; often they count as output
tokens even though your user never reads them. On your own hardware the cost
depends on context length, batch and hardware as well as on the number of
tokens. Hidden is not free.

**Latency.** This is the one that surprises teams. With a separate thinking
block, no *answer* token exists until the block closes. Assuming a constant $T$
tokens per second, a 2,000-token trace adds roughly $2000/T$ seconds of
generation before the first word of the answer; real time varies with prefill,
the growing context and server load. Measure time to first generated token
(TTFT, @sec-serving-ttft) and **time to first visible answer token**
separately. Streaming cannot speed up an answer that does not exist yet.

Whether the user stares at a blank screen for that whole interval is a separate,
product-level decision, and it varies by provider. Some services stream the
thinking separately (Anthropic's `thinking_delta` events or DeepSeek's
`reasoning_content` field, for instance), others do not expose the raw trace and
return only the answer or a summary of it; field names and visibility depend on
the model and API version, so check current documentation. The interface can
show a waiting state — a scrolling trace, a summary, or a spinner — but that
does not remove the time it takes to generate the final answer.

**Context.** The reasoning tokens generated take room in the current request's
context budget. What carries over to later turns depends on how the service
and the application keep history; a multi-turn agent that keeps its own traces
can eat its context much faster. Measure context use in long conversations
from real session logs.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The measures to track together.** At each budget, measure task performance,
total cost per problem, **cost per correct answer** — tokens spent divided by
problems solved — and latency. Accuracy alone tends to argue for spending more,
either because it genuinely rises or because its noise band is wide enough that
the largest number looks like progress. Cost per correct answer need not have
an interior minimum; the best option can sit at the edge of the measured range.
Fix the uncertainty of the success measure and the acceptable quality bar
before deciding. (That accuracy is not even reliably *increasing* is a separate
and stronger problem — @sec-cot-limits.)
:::

### Measuring the curve

Everything from here is measured, on a laptop, with a script you can rerun.
The instrument is **Qwen3-1.7B** (1,720,574,976 parameters, bfloat16, Apple
MPS). The task is **GSM8K** [@cobbe2021training], grade-school word problems
whose answers are single numbers — so scoring is exact, with no judge model in
the loop. We sample 200 problems from the test split with a fixed seed.

**Why this task, and the limits of the choice.** GSM8K is here because its
answers can be scored automatically and exactly. The curve seen on this task
should not be carried over to other datasets. The task may have become easy for
instruction-tuned models, and as an old, public test set it carries a risk of
data leakage — we did not measure contamination at the item level. Its problems
are two to eight steps deep, which is the *shallow* end of the regime
@sec-why-tokens-compute says extra depth should pay in. A harder task such as
AIME or MATH-500 may show a different budget curve — for instance a **knee**:
the point where accuracy stops rising steeply with budget and the curve
flattens, so each further token buys much less. @guo2025deepseekr1 report a
62-point swing from reinforcement learning alone on tasks of that kind. We did
not run such a sweep. The Qwen3 technical report [@yang2025qwen3] puts
Qwen3-1.7B at 13.4 on AIME'24 without thinking and 48.3 with it (73.0 and 93.4
on MATH-500), but two-mode scores like these do not by themselves show the shape
of a budget curve. AIME traces run to tens of thousands of tokens, and 200
problems × 6 budgets of that is not a laptop job. So read what follows as **"no
detectable gain on this task at this sample size"**, not as "no gain".

For each problem we sweep a
[thinking budget](#gloss-thinking-budget){#term-thinking-budget .term-ref}
across 0, 128, 256, 512, 1,024 and 2,048 tokens. Budget 0 means
`enable_thinking=False`: the same weights, answering directly. Every other
budget runs in two phases, and the mechanism matters for how you read the
results:

```text
phase 1   open thinking mode through the chat template; generate at most BUDGET tokens
          if </think> appeared, mark a natural close
          if it stopped at the cap, mark a truncation

phase 2   on a natural close keep the existing close; on a truncation add one
          generate the answer from the resulting token sequence
          (capped at 320 tokens — see the caveat below)
```

In your own harness, check at the token level whether the stop string is kept
in the generated text and that the second phase's input holds a single
`</think>`.

**Be precise about what this measures.** This chapter's local harness, if the
thinking block has not ended, cuts the trace at the set point, mid-sentence,
closes the block on the model's behalf and starts the answer phase. That is a
harsh reading of the word "budget". Providers' budget settings do not guarantee
the same semantics: some define the budget as a target rather than a strict
cap, some take an effort level rather than a token count. Check the documented
target or cap behaviour for the model version you use; whether the ceiling is
enforced by truncation, by training or by something else does not always follow
from the documentation. @muennighoff2025s1 study two interventions on an
open-weights model under the name **budget forcing**: a forced `</think>` to
cut a trace short (similar to our cut), and a *suppressed* end-of-thinking with
`Wait` appended to make the model keep going. The results they report are the
effects of those two interventions in that experiment.[^budget-api]

So read the numbers below as a **deliberately harsh truncation baseline**, not
as an estimate of what a production budget costs: this is what a naive cap does,
and a smarter policy should be measured against it. Calling it a proven
worst-case bound over all smarter policies would be a stronger claim than
anything measured here supports. We record how often the cap was hit, because a budget that
truncates 90% of traces and a budget that truncates 5% of them are different
regimes wearing the same number.

[^budget-api]: The local 128- and 256-token cuts in this chapter may have no
exact equivalent on hosted APIs. Which models support settings such as
`budget_tokens`, adaptive thinking or `effort`, and the ranges they allow, change
with the version; check the current, dated provider documentation for the model
you use. Do not equate the local experiment's results with API behaviour; what
carries over is the method for measuring the shape of the curve.

One more caveat comes before the results, because it affects how you read them.
If you would rather see the numbers first, skip the box below, read the table,
and come back.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**A limitation we found by checking our own instrument, and did not fix.**
The answer parser can change the result. This experiment reads the model's
answer as the *last number* in the text it produces. That is this chapter's
parser choice, consistent with GSM8K's gold-answer format, but another number
added after the answer can capture the score: "The answer is 72. Note this
assumes 3 items" is read as **3**, and marked wrong. Report the extraction rule
and the number of answers that failed to parse.

Which makes the 320-token ceiling on the answer phase more interesting than it
should be. Measured mean answer lengths come out between 243 and 276 tokens
against that ceiling — close enough that the cap is worth investigating, but not
close enough to tell you anything about how many answers actually hit it. A mean
of 276 is consistent with every answer being 276 tokens and none truncated, and
with a mixture of short answers and answers stopped dead at 320. We did not
record the flag that would settle it, which was a mistake in experiment design
rather than an interesting property of the model.

There is a tempting second step here, and it does not go through. Mean answer
length is **lowest in the no-thinking row** (243 tokens) and higher in *every*
thinking row (276, 267, 260, 273, 275), which looks like the penalty falling
hardest on exactly the rows being compared against the baseline. But means do not
determine cap-hit rates, so this ordering does not establish that the thinking
rows are truncated more often. It establishes that we cannot rule it out.

What we cannot do is sign the correction. Those five numbers do not move
monotonically with the budget, and neither does accuracy, so there is no clean
story of the form "the bias shrinks as the curve climbs, therefore the true gap
is larger than it looks". All we can say is that we do not know which rows are
affected or how much, that the direction of the net distortion is unknown, and
that some
unidentifiable part of this curve's shape belongs to our instrument rather than
to the model. The two cannot be separated from what we saved.

We are reporting this rather than quietly raising the cap and re-running,
because noticing that your measuring instrument has a bias is the normal
condition of doing this work, and a chapter that only ever shows clean results
would teach you the wrong lesson about what evaluation feels like. The
practical fix is one line — record whether each answer hit the ceiling, the way
we already record it for traces — and it is in the lab at the end of the
chapter so you do not repeat the mistake.
:::

Here is the sweep. Two hundred GSM8K problems, six budgets, one model, one
laptop, about seven hours of wall time. The 95% CI column is a Wilson interval,
a confidence interval for a proportion that stays sensible near 0% and 100%;
every accuracy interval in this chapter is computed the same way.

| thinking budget | accuracy | 95% CI | thinking tokens | answer tokens | total | traces cut off |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| none (`enable_thinking=False`) | 70.0% | 63.3–75.9 | 0 | 243 | 243 | — |
| 128 tokens | 61.0% | 54.1–67.5 | 125 | 276 | 401 | 97% |
| 256 tokens | 63.5% | 56.6–69.9 | 249 | 267 | 516 | 97% |
| 512 tokens | **71.5%** | 64.9–77.3 | 495 | 260 | 755 | 96% |
| 1,024 tokens | 67.5% | 60.7–73.6 | 920 | 273 | 1193 | 67% |
| 2,048 tokens | 70.0% | 63.3–75.9 | 1362 | 275 | 1637 | 28% |

Read the last row against the first before anything else. At a 2,048-token
budget the model scores **70.0%**. With thinking switched off entirely it scores
**70.0%**. The same two hundred problems, the same weights, the same seed — and
**6.74× the tokens** for a marginal difference of exactly zero.

That is the whole chapter in two rows — but before you read it as *thinking
bought nothing*, look one column to the right on that first row.

**The zero-budget row may not be a zero-reasoning row.** At a 2,048 budget and
with thinking off, point accuracy is the same, 70.0%; the mean total tokens
generated are 1,637 against 243. Thinking-off mode, too, writes **243 answer
tokens** on average to a question whose answer is a single number; how much of
that is intermediate working has to be established by reading sample answers.
This table is a cost/performance comparison between two **modes and decoding
settings**, not a pure "reasoning versus no reasoning" experiment. Hold that
against the contrast in @sec-cot-limits, where on a short label task the
no-thinking baseline writes **3.4** tokens and the token multiplier jumps from
6.74× to 88.6×.

**Now the discipline.** It would be easy to narrate the middle of this table: a
dip at 128, a recovery, a peak at 512, a wobble. Do not. Run the numbers against
the noise and every one of those stories dissolves:

```text
vs no-thinking baseline, two-proportion z-test (n=200 each)
  budget   128:  z = -1.89   NOT separable
  budget   256:  z = -1.38   NOT separable
  budget   512:  z = +0.33   NOT separable
  budget  1024:  z = -0.54   NOT separable
  budget  2048:  z = +0.00   NOT separable
```

**None of the tested budgets shows a statistically clear improvement over not
thinking at all.** The 95% interval on every row is about $\pm 7$ points wide,
and every pair of them overlaps. What the 128-token row's interval, 54.1–67.5,
does exclude is the *point estimates* 70.0 and 71.5 — and those are different
facts. Its interval still overlaps the baseline's on 63.3–67.5 and the 512
row's on 64.9–67.5. Neither containment nor overlap is a significance test:
against the baseline the two-sample test gives $z = -1.89$, which does not
reject at the 5% level, while against the 512 row it gives $z = -2.22$, which
does. Read that second number with the care it deserves — it is one uncorrected,
unpaired comparison picked out of a sweep of six, and this chapter is not
reporting it as a finding. The 512 row is bolded because it is
the largest number in the column, not because it is the best budget — at
$z = +0.33$ that bolding is decoration, and you should read it with suspicion.[^paired-test]

[^paired-test]: Because the same 200 problems were used in every condition, a
    paired comparison would have been more appropriate: McNemar's test looks only
    at the problems the two conditions disagree about and discards the concordant
    pairs they both get right or both get wrong. The two-proportion $z$-test above
    is an approximate analysis that ignores the pairing across problems; which
    way its sensitivity differs depends on the problem-level disagreements. Our
    result files saved only the per-budget mean, so McNemar's test could not be
    computed here. The lab at the end of this chapter records per-problem
    correctness at every step; in your next experiment, keep the right/wrong
    outcome of every problem under every condition.

    Two notes follow. First, the sensitivity figures in the callout below are
    computed for the *unpaired* test. The discordance rate on GSM8K is unknown;
    if the ~22% rate we measure on the classification sweep in @sec-cot-limits
    held here, the smallest difference that would reach significance at
    $n = 200$ would fall from about 9 points (unpaired) to about **6.5 points**
    (McNemar), and the difference caught at 80% power from about 12 points to
    about 9. That is an illustrative scenario, not a measurement. Second, "no
    significant difference" is not "no difference", and *exactly zero* here
    means only that the two **marginals** are equal — 140 correct out of 200 in
    both arms is compatible with dozens of problems flipping in each direction.
    Claiming equivalence needs a **TOST** (two one-sided tests against a margin
    declared in advance): a margin such as ±5 points chosen as a business
    decision *before* the sweep, and a confidence interval on the paired
    difference. Without problem-level records that claim cannot be tested here.

**What these 200 problems observe directly is the cost and the truncation.** The
token means and truncation rates in the table were observed directly for these
problems. The truncation rate is itself a proportion computed from 200 problems;
for new traffic it needs a proportion interval, and mean tokens per problem
need a problem-level bootstrap interval — we ran neither. What makes these
columns safe to read is the *size* of the differences:

- **Tokens grow monotonically and steeply:** 1.00×, 1.65×, 2.12×, 3.11×, 4.91×,
  6.74×. The difference on these 200 problems is large, but do not read it as a
  guarantee about a future bill or peak latency.
- **The truncation rate collapses in exactly the right place:** 97%, 97%, 96%,
  67%, 28%. Below 512 tokens this model is almost *never* allowed to finish
  a thought. At 2,048 most traces close on their own.

Put those two together and the accuracy column has a plausible reading — a
hypothesis, not a finding, since none of its differences is significant. The
two lowest rows (128 and 256) are rows where 97% of traces are guillotined
mid-derivation. The row that finally lets nearly three quarters of traces finish
(2,048) lands exactly back on the baseline. The 512 row does not fit the story
neatly — 96% truncated, yet the highest point estimate — which is one more
reason to treat the dips as noise until a larger or paired test says otherwise.
What the truncation column does establish is the operation itself: a hard budget
that truncates almost everything is not "less thinking" — it is a different
operation, one that hands the answer phase a half-finished derivation and asks
it to commit.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why this is not a failure of the experiment.** A reader hoping for a tidy
rising curve will find this table disappointing, but the result is not weak —
it is *clear about what it can and cannot say*. On these 200 problems the token
count rose up to 6.74× with the budget, and in the unpaired test reported no
budget separated from thinking-off mode at the 5% level. That does not rule out
a small benefit or harm.

Sensitivity is a curve, not a threshold, so quote it as one. Against a 70%
baseline at $n = 200$ per arm, $\alpha = .05$ two-sided, unpaired: this design
has **80% power to detect a 12-point gain and 90% power to detect a 14-point
one**. A genuine 9-point gain it would catch about half the time; a 5-point gain
one time in five. (A *drop* of the same size is caught slightly less often,
because the variance of a proportion grows as it moves towards 50%.) These
figures are **a planning calculation under the assumption of two independent
proportions**; the real power of the paired design cannot be set without the
problem-level results we did not save. The honest statement is therefore not
"there is no effect" but *this design would probably miss a five-point effect
and would usually catch a twelve-point one*. Turning a failure to reject into a
positive claim of equivalence needs a different test again — see the footnote
above.

That is a genuinely useful finding to carry into a procurement conversation. "It
might help a little, we cannot tell, and here is the bill" is the honest answer,
and it is the one most reasoning-model deployments actually deserve.
:::

### Pricing it yourself

Price per token depends on *your* contract or *your* hardware. Cost per correct
answer depends on that and also on the model's task performance, the input and
output lengths and your retry pattern, so the last step has to be a calculator
rather than a claim. The tool below combines the measured GSM8K points with the
output-token price you choose: the points are ours, the two sliders are yours.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
budgetRows = [
  {budget: 0, acc: 70.0, total_tok: 243, capped: 0},
  {budget: 128, acc: 61.0, total_tok: 401, capped: 97},
  {budget: 256, acc: 63.5, total_tok: 516, capped: 97},
  {budget: 512, acc: 71.5, total_tok: 755, capped: 96},
  {budget: 1024, acc: 67.5, total_tok: 1193, capped: 67},
  {budget: 2048, acc: 70.0, total_tok: 1637, capped: 28}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tokPrice = Inputs.range([0.05, 20], { value: 2.0, step: 0.05, label: "Price per 1M output tokens (USD)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tps = Inputs.range([10, 600], { value: 120, step: 5, label: "Single-request decode speed (tokens/second)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
budgetCost = budgetRows.map(d => {
  const costPer1k = (d.total_tok * 1000 * tokPrice) / 1e6;
  const solved1k = (d.acc / 100) * 1000;
  return {
    ...d,
    label: d.budget === 0 ? "no thinking" : `${d.budget.toLocaleString()} tokens`,
    costPer1k,
    perCorrect: solved1k > 0 ? costPer1k / solved1k : NaN, // point estimate; accuracy's ±7-point interval has to be read separately
    latency: d.total_tok / tps
  };
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Observable Plot cannot resolve a CSS variable, so read the theme once here.
// The SVGs in this chapter already do the right thing through --fig-*; this
// cell and the table below it were the exception, and #5B6272 label text sits
// at 2.5:1 on the dark background.
figColor = name => getComputedStyle(document.documentElement)
  .getPropertyValue(`--fig-${name}`).trim() || "currentColor"
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 680,
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 66,
  marginBottom: 46,
  ariaLabel: "Cost per correct answer against tokens generated per problem, one point per thinking budget",
  x: { label: "average tokens generated per problem", grid: true },
  y: { label: "USD per correct answer", grid: true, zero: true },
  marks: [
    Plot.line(budgetCost, { x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2 }),
    Plot.dot(budgetCost, {
      x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", r: 5,
      fill: d => d.perCorrect === d3.min(budgetCost, v => v.perCorrect) ? figColor("rose") : figColor("navy"),
      title: d => `${d.label}\n${d.acc.toFixed(1)}% correct\n${d.total_tok.toFixed(0)} tokens\n$${d.perCorrect.toFixed(4)} per correct answer`
    }),
    Plot.text(budgetCost, {
      x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", text: "label",
      dy: -14, fontSize: 11, fill: figColor("muted")
    })
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}

  </tr>`)}
</table>
<p style="font-size:0.85rem; color:var(--fig-muted); margin-top:8px">
The highlighted row is the lowest cost-per-correct ratio computed from these six
points' <b>measured accuracy estimates</b> and the output-token price chosen. The
token counts are measured; the accuracies are point estimates that each carry a
confidence interval of roughly ±7 points, so the highlight is not a declaration
of a statistical winner. Note what the price slider cannot change: it scales
every row identically, so <b>the cheapest budget does not move as the price
moves</b>. What the price changes is how much the wrong choice costs you.
<br><br>
That invariance is narrow. This calculator charges for output tokens only. Add
input cost, a per-request fee or different tariffs and the ranking has to be
recomputed; the direction of any shift is not guaranteed in advance and depends
on the accuracy levels and the gaps between points. Likewise the seconds column
approximates generation time at the fixed tokens-per-second rate chosen; it
leaves out prefill, queueing, batching and varying decode speed, so do not read
it as a capacity estimate.</p>`
```

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**One task, one model, one prompt format.** This curve is Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K,
and it is worth being explicit that **we did not get the textbook shape**. The
canonical picture — cheap early gains, a knee, then a flat tail — is what the
literature reports for large models. Our small model instead spent its first two
non-zero budgets *below* the baseline and its last one exactly on it.

This curve does not directly contradict the 2022 experiments with
prompt-elicited chain of thought (@sec-cot-two-ways), but Qwen3-1.7B has a
different training and template regime, so that paper's parameter threshold
cannot explain it either. The high truncation rate at the 128- and 256-token
budgets is an explanation to be tested for the lower point accuracy observed
there: at those budgets 97% of traces were being severed mid-derivation. But
neither dip is statistically separable from the baseline, and the 512 row,
truncated at a similar rate, coming out higher rules out a single-cause reading.

So take two things from this table and leave the third. Take the *method*, and
take the discovery that the honest answer can be "no detectable difference, at
this price". Do not take the location of a knee — we did not find one, and on
your task and model you may well find that the curve genuinely climbs.
@sec-cot-limits runs the same sweep on a task where it should not.
:::

## Spending the budget sideways: self-consistency, verifiers, and search {#sec-parallel-compute}

@sec-budgets bought computation in one direction only: a longer trace. A
different option is to generate several independent candidates and combine
their answers. **Eight 250-token attempts**, for example, equal one 2,000-token
attempt only *in the thinking-token cap*; the eight answers' tokens, the
repeated prefill of the input, the combining step and the latency can all
differ. The failure profile is completely different.

This is the axis many teams never try. Which one wins you cannot know without
measuring, since the best strategy depends on how hard the question is
[@snell2025scaling, below]. Compare serial and parallel sampling on the tokens
actually spent, price, latency and task performance.

### Why more attempts help at all

The reason lies in how *errors* are distributed, not in the model, and it is
worth stating precisely because it also tells you when the trick fails.

Sample the same problem several times at a non-zero temperature and you may get
different reasoning paths; how varied they are depends on the model and the
temperature. Different paths sometimes reach the same correct result:

- On a numerical problem **the right answer is usually a single value**; paths
  that reason correctly land on the same number.
- Wrong answers **can scatter**: a dropped sign, a misread quantity, an
  arithmetic slip in step four can each produce a *different* wrong number. But
  wrong answers can also pile up systematically on the same value.

If the wrong answers are scattered, picking the most frequent answer can help;
if they pile up on one value, the majority vote misleads. Agreement on its own
is not evidence. @wang2023selfconsistency studied this strategy as
*self-consistency*. Before voting, measure how answers are normalised and on
which errors they converge.

"The same answer" is a rule you have to define before the task, and this is
where most self-consistency implementations quietly lose their gains: `72` and
`72.5` are different votes; `72` and `72.0` can denote the same number; `$72`
and `72 TL` are not the same answer, because the currency differs. Build a
normaliser that handles number format, unit, range and tolerance separately and
measure its errors on a validation set; that unglamorous piece of engineering
has a large effect on the number you report.

A little binomial arithmetic shows how strong the effect is, and in which
direction it runs. Take the simplest case: each sample is right with
probability $p$, independently, and every wrong sample gives the *same* wrong
answer, so the vote is a straight two-way contest. With $p = 0.6$, the chance
that the majority is right is 60% for one sample, 68.3% for five and 73.3% for
nine, and it keeps climbing towards 100% as you add samples. With $p = 0.4$ the
same arithmetic runs backwards: 40%, 31.7%, 26.7%, falling towards zero.
Voting does not make a model better. It makes the model's *most likely* answer
more certain to be returned. With many different wrong answers the decision
goes to the answer with the most votes: the correct answer only has to beat the
largest single wrong answer, not all of them combined, and if it comes up more
often than each wrong answer individually, more votes help. This arithmetic
assumes independent samples; measure the real model's error distribution and
sample diversity separately.

Say that backwards, because the backwards form is the operational one: **if your
task's wrong answers can agree with each other, self-consistency will confidently
amplify the error.** A model with a systematic bias — a units convention it
often misreads, a Turkish negation suffix it often misses — keeps voting for the
same wrong answer. If that answer comes up on 60% of samples, the right one on
30% and others on 10%, then with eight independent votes the wrong answer takes
the most votes outright about 75% of the time; break ties at random and it is
chosen about 81% of the time (the exact figure depends on the tie rule), and
more often as $k$ grows. Self-consistency does not fix the model's shared
mistakes; it can turn a mistake made on most samples into one the system makes
almost every time. You get no warning; a clear majority looks exactly like
confidence.

### What the original paper found

@wang2023selfconsistency sampled 40 reasoning paths per problem and took the
majority answer. On GSM8K with PaLM-540B this moved accuracy from **56.5% with
greedy chain-of-thought decoding to 74.4%**. That $+17.9$-point gain needed
no new training, but it was not free: it came at the cost of generating 40
samples and matching their answers. The gains were
smaller but consistent elsewhere: on GPT-3 code-davinci-002, SVAMP rose from
75.8% to 86.8% and AQuA from 39.8% to 52.0%.[^sc-models]

[^sc-models]: Worth a footnote because it is easy to garble: the +11.0 and
+12.2 deltas quoted above are code-davinci-002, not PaLM-540B. PaLM-540B's own
SVAMP gain is $+7.6$ (79.0 → 86.6). Only the GSM8K figure of $+17.9$ happens to
hold for both models. This is the kind of detail that gets flattened in
secondary write-ups, and flattening it would make the technique look more
uniform than it is.

The number to design around, though, is not the headline. It is the **shape**.
The paper sweeps 1, 5, 10, 20 and 40 paths and reports that "in most cases the
performance saturates quickly", recommending you "try a small number of paths
(e.g., 5 or 10) ... to realize most of the gains".

Within the range the paper sweeps, most of the gain arrives with the first
samples. That shows the average value of an extra sample can fall; it does not
give a hard zero-gain threshold for every task. Cost grows roughly linearly in
$k$ — every path is a full generation — though batching and fixed costs can make
it less than strictly linear. The right $k$ is set by the accuracy difference,
the total generation cost and the latency target together. Which raises the
obvious question: for a small model, on a real task, how much do extra samples
buy?

### Our measurement: what the fifth sample is worth

Asserting that majority voting saturates is easy. The curve is rarely plotted,
so here it is. We take the first 120 of the same GSM8K problems, fix a 512-token
thinking budget, and generate $k = 5$ answers per problem with different random
seeds. Because the sampler shuffles with a fixed seed and we take a prefix, these
120 are a genuine subset of the 200 used elsewhere. Then we compute majority@$k$
offline for every $k$ from 1 to 5, on **prefixes of the same five samples**. The
data and sample selection therefore do not change between arms; the curve is
still the outcome of this one draw of five samples and of the tie-break rule.

We planned eight samples and stopped at five, which is worth reporting because
the reason is a cost this chapter had otherwise missed. **Wall-clock time did
not scale the way the token count says it should.** The sequential sweep managed
0.28 minutes per problem at a 512-token budget; this run averaged **1.43**
minutes per problem per sample at the same budget, on the same machine, with the
same decoding settings, and none of that difference is visible in the token
*count*. Five passes over 120 problems took **14 hours**.[^slowdown] Since we
could not measure the cause, we do not apply that ratio to other conditions.

[^slowdown]: The range is honest rather than sloppy: the first three samples
    averaged 1.15 minutes per problem and the last two 1.85, on a laptop that had
    by then been generating continuously for half a day. We cannot cleanly
    attribute the gap: thermal and memory-pressure drift over a 14-hour run
    explains part of it, and we did not instrument the rest, so we quote both
    ends rather than a mechanism. The comparison against 0.28 survives either
    way, which is the only part the argument needs — and *"we measured it and
    cannot explain it"* is a better thing to publish than a plausible story.

When planning multi-sample runs, record token counts and wall-clock time
separately, and in a short pilot try to hold model load, device temperature,
batch and prompt length fixed. Multiplying the single-trace time by $k$ would
have underestimated the real time in this run.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This run does not compare serial and multi-sample decoding at equal cost.**
Five 512-token attempts, at the roughly 755 total tokens per problem measured in
@sec-budgets, come to about $5 \times 755 = 3{,}775$ output tokens; the single
2,048-token run produced 1,637. So even if majority@5 beats the deepest
sequential row here, that is *not* evidence that parallel beats sequential; it
is a more expensive arm winning.

The lab's (@sec-reasoning-lab) `8 × 256` against `1 × 2048` comparison also
equalises only the thinking **caps**: with the table's means, total output is
roughly $8 \times 516 = 4{,}128$ tokens against 1,637 — about 2.5×, before the
repeated prompt prefill and any verifier calls. That is arithmetic on the table,
not a re-measurement. For a real equalisation, adjust the number of candidates
and their caps until the **measured total tokens or money spent** match, and
count the prefill of the reused prompt and the combining step separately. We
report the saturation curve because the point here is the *shape* of the
aggregation; where the two strategies cross at equal cost is a question this run
was not designed to answer.

**And one more thing it does not isolate.** At a 512-token budget 96% of our
traces are truncated (@sec-budgets), so this multi-sample result does not
generalise to completed traces. Truncation may also be a shared cause of error
across the five samples; whether it raises or lowers the self-consistency gain
cannot be determined from these data. When re-measuring at a higher budget,
record the total cost and the problem-level shared errors too; even the 28%
truncation rate of the 2,048 budget in @sec-budgets is not an "untruncated"
condition.
:::

| samples $k$ | majority@$k$ | 95% CI | gain over $k=1$ | any-correct@$k$ | left on the table |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 73.3% | 64.8–80.4 | +0.0 | 73.3% | 0.0 |
| 2 | 73.3% | 64.8–80.4 | +0.0 | 81.7% | 8.3 |
| 3 | 77.5% | 69.2–84.1 | +4.2 | 83.3% | 5.8 |
| 4 | 75.8% | 67.4–82.6 | +2.5 | 85.8% | 10.0 |
| 5 | 76.7% | 68.3–83.3 | +3.3 | 85.8% | 9.2 |

Three things in that table are worth more than the headline.

**First, the honest headline itself.** Five samples bought $+3.3$ points, and
that is not separable from zero:

```text
majority@1 vs majority@5, McNemar (paired, same 120 problems)
  right@1 wrong@5: 2     wrong@1 right@5: 6
  chi-sq(1) = 1.12   <  3.841        NOT separable at p = .05
```

Every McNemar figure in this chapter uses Edwards' continuity correction,
$\chi^2 = (|b-c|-1)^2/(b+c)$, which is the conservative convention; without it
the three values we report would read 2.00, 15.36 and 11.66 instead of 1.12,
14.20 and 10.78. None of the conclusions change, but you cannot reproduce the
arithmetic without knowing which formula produced it.

On 120 problems majority@5 fixed six problems relative to the first sample and
broke two ($b = 2$, $c = 6$): a point difference of $+3.3$. With only eight
discordant problems the uncertainty is large, and the paired test does not
separate the difference at the 5% level. The direction agrees with the original
paper, but this small run does not on its own show a reliable positive effect,
and the curve wobbling *down* at $k=4$ before coming back up is what
noise looks like at this sample size. Self-consistency is a well-replicated
result and nothing here contradicts it — but our own run is not the evidence.

**Second, the $k=2$ row is not a fluke; it teaches this implementation's tie rule.** Its gain
is exactly $+0.0$, and we verified it is exactly $+0.0$ per problem: majority@2
gave the same answer as majority@1 on **120 of 120**. That is the result of
**this tie-break rule**, not luck. With two votes you either get agreement — in which case the winner is the
answer sample 1 already gave — or a $1\!-\!1$ tie, which any implementation must
break somehow, and `collections.Counter` breaks it towards the first sample.
Under this rule, either way you paid for a second full generation and could not
have changed the outcome; random or verifier-assisted tie-breaking can give a
different result.[^tie-break]

[^tie-break]: The specific tie-break matters less than the parity. Break ties
    randomly and $k=2$ stops being a strict no-op, but it still buys you a coin
    flip on the 28% of problems where the two samples disagree, which is not
    what anyone means by "voting". **Prefer odd $k$.** The general shape is that
    going from $2m$ to $2m{+}1$ samples buys real tie-breaking power while
    $2m{-}1$ to $2m$ buys comparatively little — visible here as the dip at
    $k=4$.

**Third — and this is the column to actually design around — look at what voting
throws away.** By $k=5$ the correct answer was somewhere in the five samples
**85.8%** of the time. Voting extracted **76.7%**. The last column is the
difference: **9.2 points that the model had already computed and paid for, and
that counting discarded.**

In this table `any-correct@`$k$ is the rate at which at least one of exactly
these $k$ answers is right; `majority@`$k$ is the accuracy of the answer the
vote returns. The first is close to the idea of *coverage* reported as
**pass@$k$** in code-generation work, but papers often report pass@$k$ with an
unbiased estimator computed from $n > k$ samples rather than from exactly $k$,
and sampling protocols differ [@chen2021evaluating]. Do not compare your own
any-correct@$k$ with those numbers directly. Define the voting result under one
name (elsewhere it may appear as cons@$k$ or maj@$k$) and use it consistently.
Reporting only one of the two hides which part of the gain came from the model
and which from the aggregator.

At least one of the five candidates was right on 85.8% of problems; voting
picked the right answer on 76.7%. The 9.2 points between them are the largest
gap a perfect selector could close **for this candidate set and this scorer**,
and that is the business case for the next section. How much of it a real
verifier closes needs a separate experiment, and on 120 problems the gap itself
carries sampling uncertainty.

**Before you train anything, though, try weighting the votes you already have.**
Majority voting treats five samples as five equal ballots. If the model exposes
log-probabilities, you can try the log-probability of the answer tokens or of
the trace as a weight; @wang2023selfconsistency report a variant of this kind in
the original paper. That information is unavailable on some APIs, storing and
computing it has a cost, and a high probability is not a calibrated estimate of
correctness, so test it together with length effects. Temper the expectation:
in their own experiments, weighting by the length-normalised probability of
each path scored about the same as plain majority voting. Another label-free
option is to hand the $k$ candidates *back* to the model and ask it to pick; it
gives you a selector for free-form answers that have no equality test, but adds
prompt and generation cost. The trained verifier below is the *third* thing to
try, not the second. Compare the methods on held-out data.

### When you can score, do not vote

Majority voting uses only the candidates' matched *final answers* and ignores
everything the model wrote to get there. If you have a checker that scores a
candidate's correctness **reliably**, that extra information can make for a
better choice.

A [verifier](#gloss-verifier){#term-verifier .term-ref} can be a learned model,
an executable test or a rule. @cobbe2021training introduced GSM8K together with
re-ranking many candidates by a learned verifier: sample many solutions, score
each, return the best. The recipe is now usually called **best-of-$N$**: $N$
samples, one scorer, keep the top one. A poor or off-task scorer can do worse
than counting votes; compare the scorer and the vote on the same candidates.

::: {#gloss-verifier .column-margin .term-gloss}
**verifier** — a rule, an executable test or a learned scorer that checks a
candidate answer or solution. Among learned ones, an **ORM** (*outcome reward
model*) is trained on the final result of a solution and a **PRM** (*process
reward model*) on labels given to intermediate steps. The reliability of both
has to be measured separately on training data and on out-of-task examples.
[↩](#term-verifier){.term-back}
:::

@cobbe2021training report that a roughly 6B model generating many candidates
and selecting with a verifier "slightly outperforms a finetuned 175B model" in
their GSM8K setting, "a boost approximately equivalent to a 30x model size
increase". The "about 30×" is only the ratio of parameter counts; it says
nothing of the same ratio for the total inference compute, latency or serving
cost of 100 candidates.

@lightman2024verify then asked what the verifier should be trained to judge.
Scoring the *final answer* is
**outcome supervision**; scoring *each step* is **process supervision**. On a
500-problem subset of MATH, selecting the best of 1,860 samples:

| selection method | MATH problems solved |
|:--|--:|
| majority voting (self-consistency) | 69.6% |
| outcome-supervised verifier | 72.4% |
| process-supervised verifier | **78.2%** |

On this MATH subset and the same candidate pool, the process-supervised selector
beat the outcome-supervised one, and both beat majority voting
[@lightman2024verify]. That ordering does not carry over to another task
automatically; even at equal generation cost, the cost of process labels and of
running the scorer at test time belongs in the total. The paper's explanation
is that step-level labels "provide more precise feedback than outcome
supervision", and that "the marginal value of a negative label from outcome
supervision is low": knowing a 40-step solution ended wrong tells you little
about which step to blame.

The distinction that matters in practice is **what you supervise**:

| | outcome supervision | process supervision |
|:--|:--|:--|
| what the label covers | correctness of the final result | local correctness of an intermediate step |
| possible label source | a test, a rule or a person | a person, a rule or automatic rollouts |
| benefit | can be cheap and tied directly to the result | can flag a faulty step earlier |
| limit | can miss a right result reached by a wrong path | step labels can be wrong; local correctness does not guarantee the final solution |

The labelling-cost argument is not absolute either: methods that produce step
labels with rollouts instead of people — completing the solution several times
after each step and checking how often it reaches the right answer (e.g.
Math-Shepherd) — make process supervision much cheaper.

Outcome supervision has a specific pathology that connects straight back to
@sec-faithfulness: a solution that reasons wrongly and arrives at the right
number receives full credit. Train on enough of those and you risk
selecting for reasoning that does not have to be sound.[^uesato]

[^uesato]: @uesato2022solving compare outcome and process supervision on
    GSM8K; they found the two roughly tied on final-answer accuracy, with process
    supervision better on their *reasoning*-error measure. Read final accuracy
    and the reasoning-error measure separately. @lightman2024verify report a PRM
    advantage on a different maths set and candidate setup. Together the two
    show that process supervision can help **in these experiments**; it does not
    guarantee both the right answer and a faithful rationale on every task.

### Searching with the verifier, not just re-ranking with it

Everything so far generates first and chooses afterwards. Best-of-$N$ samples
$N$ complete solutions and picks one; voting does the same without a scorer.
**Search** is the third option, and it is the one the section title promised:
choose *while* you generate.

The mechanism is a beam search over steps rather than over tokens: expand
partial solutions and select by a score. Generate the first step $M$ ways,
score each partial solution (a process-supervised verifier is one option; a
rule-based checker or the model's own judgement can also be used), keep the
best $b$, expand only those, repeat. *Lookahead* search is
the same loop with one extra rollout per candidate before scoring, trading
compute for a less myopic score. @yao2023tree is the prompt-level cousin of
this — a tree of candidate thoughts with the model itself asked to evaluate
them. It is one thing to try when you have no trained scorer, but the model can
score itself wrongly, so it is neither the only option nor a guaranteed
improvement.

Why it can beat re-ranking at the same budget: a partial path can be dropped
where it goes wrong rather than forty steps later, **if the scorer catches the
error**, which saves the cost of generating the full solution. If the scorer
misjudges, a correct path can be pruned too. That is the search-side statement
of @lightman2024verify's observation that the marginal value of a negative
outcome label is low. A PRM is a suitable tool for partial solutions; a checker
that can only look at the final result does not give the same information
directly without extra completions (rollouts).

Why it does not always win, and the two costs to price before you build it.
@snell2025scaling's central finding — the one the next subsection is about — is
that the best strategy depends on how hard the question is. Verifier-guided
beam search beat best-of-$N$ on medium-difficulty problems, but on easy ones it
over-optimised the verifier at larger budgets — it found steps the verifier
scored highly that were not actually better — and plain best-of-$N$ did better;
on the hardest problems neither made much progress. Easy questions also
gained most from purely sequential revision. So committing to one strategy in
advance leaves efficiency on the table; re-test the ordering with your own
candidate pool and scorer. And in a search, successive **levels** depend on each
other, which adds waiting and a scorer pass per candidate per step. Candidates
on the same level can still be batched. Best-of-$N$ lends itself better to
generating full answers concurrently, but its latency too depends on capacity
and batch efficiency.

### How far this actually goes

@snell2025scaling is the paper usually cited for "test-time compute beats making
the model bigger", and it is worth citing accurately, because the popular
version of the claim drops the half that constrains it.

The efficiency result has a scope: on the paper's maths problems and base
model, choosing *how* to spend test-time compute by question difficulty improves
"the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4× compared to a
best-of-N baseline". That is not a general ratio for all inference scaling. The
FLOP-matched comparison against pretraining is explicitly conditional too; there
are settings where the small model with extra inference beats the larger one,
but the relationship shifts. Test-time
compute wins "on the easy questions or in settings with a lower inference load";
pretraining wins "on the harder questions or in settings with a higher inference
load". And on the hardest problems they observe "very little benefits from
scaling up test-time compute".

Their own summary is the sentence to take away: **"Test-time and pretraining
compute are not 1-to-1 'exchangeable'."**

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The cost choice depends on the workload.** A smaller model may meet the quality
bar with extra inference compute. High traffic makes per-request compute
matter; switching to a stronger off-the-shelf model, routing requests or
investing in training are separate cost options. Not every product can
realistically train its own model either: training needs data, hardware,
maintenance and amortisation. Which is cheaper is set by your task mix, traffic
volume, accuracy target and maintenance cost.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Every method needs a comparison signal.** Voting has to be able to match
candidate answers; a verifier has to be able to score candidates; search has to
be able to rank partial paths. An automatic, exact correctness check is a strong
signal, but for tasks such as "summarise this contract", "write a polite Turkish
reply to this complaint" or "is this review positive" with a nuanced middle,
human judgement, a task metric or a learned scorer can be used. Evaluate those
signals' error rates separately. Test-time compute is easiest to buy where
correctness is cheap to check, but do not load the same **narrow** condition as
the verifiable-reward setting in @sec-cot-two-ways onto all three methods.
:::

### The decision, compressed

Four ways of spending a token budget, and no single winner. The table below is a
starting point for comparing serial generation, multiple sampling, verifiers
and search. Alongside whether you can compare answers, measure the budget,
latency, candidate diversity and scorer error.

| your situation | spend it on | why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| you can compare answers, latency has slack | try multiple sampling | the vote concentrates on the model's most likely answer; the benefit depends on how the candidates' errors are distributed |
| you can compare answers; latency is tight, **the server has spare capacity** | concurrent (batched) sampling | measure the latency gain under batching and queueing; it also spends your fleet's capacity |
| the task needs long derivations | a longer single trace | later steps may depend on earlier ones |
| you can *execute* the answer | run it — tests, a solver, a unit check | the cheapest verifier is often not a model |
| you have reliable labelled solutions or a scorer | compare the verifier with voting on the same candidates | scorer error and extra cost decide the outcome |
| you have candidates but no separate scorer | where possible, try probability weighting or re-selection by the model | confidence calibration and extra-call cost have to be measured |
| answers are free-form text | define a task-appropriate similarity or quality measure | a single perfect reference is not required; check the measure's error |
| the model is *systematically* wrong | change the prompt, the data or add external checking | voting over more samples from the same model can entrench the error |

## Where reasoning helps, and where it only burns tokens {#sec-cot-limits}

This section looks at which tasks thinking mode helps on, and at what cost. On
tasks such as maths and symbolic manipulation extra steps can help; on short
classification and formatting jobs the return on the same cost can be smaller
or unclear. Switching to a reasoning model does not upgrade everything by
itself. We look at the literature's results first and then compare the Turkish
sentiment-classification experiment under its own conditions — which is why this
section ends with us measuring it rather than quoting it.

The honest version is a question with two parts, and you can answer both before
writing any code.

### The two questions that decide it

**Can the task benefit from extra serial computation?** @sec-why-tokens-compute
said extra tokens can buy serial depth. Tasks such as multi-step arithmetic,
multi-constraint scheduling, code that has to satisfy an invariant or a proof
can benefit from intermediate results. A competent human reaching for scratch
paper is a useful intuition, but it does not prove the model needs the same
number of visible intermediate tokens. Measure the effect against a direct
answer.

If the answer is a **judgement about the input as a whole** — is this review
positive, is this email spam, which of five categories is this ticket — the task
can often be solved with a short answer, and a long thinking block's benefit is
not automatic. Test separately, on subsets with negation, several conditions or
ambiguous context, whether extra steps help. Unneeded generation can add both
cost and error risk: it gives the model 500 tokens in which to talk itself out
of a correct first impression.

**What signal can you compare candidates with?** Every part of
@sec-parallel-compute — voting, verifiers, search — needs a notion of "the same
answer" or "a better answer". A cheap automatic check of the right answer is the
strongest case. Without one, answer equivalence, a task rubric, a learned scorer
or human evaluation can be used; their extra cost and error are part of the
decision. This question is independent of the first and has to be weighed
together with it.
